summary: The whole people gathers 'as one man' at the water-gate and asks Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses. He reads from sunrise to noon; the people say Amen with lifted hands, weep — and are told not to mourn, because the day is holy: go eat the fat and drink the sweet, and send portions to those who have nothing. The next day they discover the feast of booths in the law and keep it for the first time since Joshua.
whyItMatters: This is the rebirth of public Scripture reading — the moment the community becomes a people of the Book. And its first lesson is emotional: conviction is real, but the holy response ends in joy and shared food, not in endless tears.

context.author: Nehemiah's memoir, featuring Ezra the scribe
context.audience: All the returned community — 'men and women, and every one who had understanding'
context.date: First day of the seventh month, 445/444 BC (the Feast of Trumpets)
context.setting: The broad open square before the water-gate, east Jerusalem

outline.heading: The gathering and the request
outline.note: The people ask for the law — revival starts with hunger

outline.heading: The reading

keyVerses.text: And all the people were gathered as one man to the broad place before the water-gate, and they told Esdras the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the Lord commanded Israel.
keyVerses.why: The people asked. No decree, no compulsion — hunger for the word came first.

keyVerses.text: And Esdras blessed the Lord, the great God: and all the people answered, and said, Amen, lifting up their hands: and they bowed down and worshipped the Lord with their face to the ground.
keyVerses.why: The posture of a receiving congregation — standing, hands raised, faces down. Much of later synagogue and church liturgy grows from this scene.

keyVerses.text: Go, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions to them that have nothing; for the day is holy to our Lord: and faint not, for the Lord is our strength.
keyVerses.why: Holy-day joy with a social edge: celebration is incomplete until the poor are included.

keyVerses.text: For the children of Israel had not done so from the days of Jesus the son of Naue until that day: and there was great joy.
keyVerses.why: A thousand-year gap — the feast of booths had not been kept like this since Joshua. 'Jesus son of Naue' is Brenton's Greek form of Joshua son of Nun.

questions.question: Who is Esdras, and why does he appear so late in this book?
questions.answer: Esdras is Ezra — the scribe and priest whose own memoir filled the earlier chapters of this combined book. In the 23-chapter Septuagint arrangement his earlier work sits before Nehemiah's memoir; here the two leaders appear together, Ezra teaching and Nehemiah governing.

questions.question: Why did the people weep when they heard the law?
questions.answer: They heard the covenant they had broken — and how far their practice had drifted. The leaders' response is striking: this is a holy day, stop mourning. Conviction has its moment; then joy is commanded, because 'the Lord is our strength.'

questions.question: What does 'they understood the law in the reading' mean — did they translate it?
questions.answer: The returnees' everyday language had shifted toward Aramaic; the Hebrew text needed explanation. The Levites read, then 'instructed them distinctly' — giving the sense. This is the root of the synagogue's reading-plus-explanation pattern, and of preaching itself.

questions.question: What is the feast of booths?
questions.answer: Sukkot — seven days living in makeshift shelters of branches, remembering the wilderness years when Israel lived in tents with God in the middle of the camp. Finding it in the law, the people built booths on rooftops and courtyards the very next day.

questions.question: Why does joy get commanded?
questions.answer: Because grief had done its work and could become its own performance. 'Faint not, for the Lord is our strength' — the day's holiness is expressed in eating, drinking, and sending portions to the poor. In this book, repentance always aims at joy.

glossary.def: The Greek form of Ezra; 'the scribe' means a scholar and copyist of the law.
A gate on the eastern slope, near the Gihon spring — its open square held crowds.
Temporary shelters of branches; the feast of Sukkot (tabernacles).
Brenton's Greek form of Joshua son of Nun, Moses' successor.
